**No.** If you're asking whether to start a startup in college, Paul Graham's answer is no. But keep building the side project, because that's exactly what he'd tell you to do.

**What he's said**

- **The rule.** In *Before the Startup* (2014), a talk he gave to Stanford students, he says it directly: "Do not start a startup in college." His reason is that "you can't start a startup for real as a student, because if you start a startup for real you're not a student anymore."
- **Why age 20 matters.** He thinks "most people should still be searching breadth-first at 20." He also argues that the danger is succeeding, not failing: "If you start a startup at 20 and you're sufficiently successful, you'll never get to do it." In a 2018 interview he called starting that young "premature optimization." He said "it's good to mess around with a whole bunch of things in your early 20s," and that a startup that works is "like catching a dragon by the tail."
- **Startups are a poor way to learn.** In 2025 he wrote that "the point of a startup is to make something people want, not to learn," and that "the way to learn the fastest is to work on whatever you're most curious about."

**Why your side project still matters**

In the same essay he says "the best startups almost have to start as side projects." Apple, Yahoo, Google and Facebook all began as projects that weren't meant to be companies. He also gives the exception: if you're 20 and a side project "takes off like Facebook did… it may be reasonable to run with it." The thing he objects to is deliberately turning yourself into a startup founder at 20, which he calls "gratuitously stupid."

**What to do**

Keep working on the project because it interests you, not as a company. Don't incorporate it, raise money, or drop classes because you're excited. Do those things only if users show up and keep growing faster than you can handle. At that point the project has made the choice for you, and Graham would say to run with it. Excitement alone doesn't count as that signal. Users pulling the product out of your hands does.

Sources:
- [Paul Graham, "Before the Startup"](https://paulgraham.com/before.html)
- [TechCrunch: Paul Graham on why he doesn't like seeing college-age and younger founders (2018)](https://techcrunch.com/2018/09/01/paul-graham-on-why-he-doesnt-like-seeing-college-age-and-younger-founders)
- [Fortune: YC cofounder says high school isn't the time to start a startup (2025)](https://fortune.com/2025/09/08/yc-cofounder-gen-z-warning-high-school-not-time-to-start-startup-reddit-airbnb-dropbox)
- [Paul Graham, "What You'll Wish You'd Known"](https://paulgraham.com/hs.html), on self-chosen side projects

They kept it free and unsponsored because the audience they wanted, actual and would-be startup founders, had almost no money, and they wanted the day to be only about the talks.

**Money was what founders lacked.** Livingston said so directly in her 2008 post: "The event is free, because we know that the one thing most startup founders lack is money." She wrote that it "always seemed odd" to her that so many web conferences charged so much to attend. She also pointed out that the people priced out of those events were often the ones at the center of new developments on the web. Charging admission would have screened out the people they most wanted in the room.

**They wanted nothing but content.** Her description of the event: "no sponsors, no introductory remarks, no exhibitors, no bags full of schwag." There were bagels and coffee in the morning "and not much else." She called it an experiment to see "how much we could give everyone for free in one concentrated day of talks." Sponsors would have brought exhibitors, sales pitches and stage time, which is exactly what they had left out on purpose.

**The goal was education, not revenue.** In "Why I Love Startup School," she says they "simply wanted to educate people," because more people might see starting a startup as a career option if they knew more about it. They modeled the first event (Harvard, fall 2005) on Graham's Spam Conference, which was cheap and focused on content. The speakers came in on a Saturday, unpaid, "just to help future founders."

In short, sponsors and ticket fees would have made the event worse for the people it was meant to reach, so they left both out. I didn't find a reason stated by Graham himself; everything above is from Livingston's own posts.

Sources:
- [Startup School 2008 – Founders at Work (Jessica Livingston)](http://www.foundersatwork.com/blog/startup-school-2008)
- [Why I Love Startup School – Jessica Livingston](https://foundersatwork.posthaven.com/why-i-love-startup-school)

**My answer: start, but only after you can say why you'll win.** Nothing I found shows Caldwell treating a dominant product as a reason to stay out. What he does warn about is founders who haven't studied the market they're entering.

**What he has said:**

- **Assume your idea isn't original, and research who came before.** At YC he told applicants that "your startup idea is probably less original than you think." He urged them to "see how many people have tried it before you." His advice for crowded spaces was: "try to show that you know more or have done more work" than everyone else there. ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2022/04/27/how-to-get-into-y-combinator-dalton-caldwell/))
- **Fit matters more than novelty.** Finding "an idea that fits you like a glove" counts for more than being original, and he looks for founder/market fit, such as having worked in the field. ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2022/04/27/how-to-get-into-y-combinator-dalton-caldwell/))
- **Watch for "tar pit" ideas.** These are ideas that look easy and appealing but that thousands of founders have already failed at. His example is music discovery, which "probably tens of thousands of founders" have tried. The real warning sign is an apparent gap that keeps trapping people, not a strong incumbent. ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2022/04/27/how-to-get-into-y-combinator-dalton-caldwell/), [Lenny's Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/lessons-from-1000-yc-startups))
- **Newcomers have a structural advantage.** He has tweeted: "A brand new startup with no traction has a non-obvious edge over an established startup with sunk costs on something that isn't working." ([X](https://x.com/daltonc/status/1598716876498305024))
- **He also did it himself.** In 2012 he launched App.net as a paid, ad-free, developer-friendly alternative to Twitter, which dominated the market. He positioned it as fixing what he saw as Twitter's mistakes, not copying it. ([MIT Technology Review](https://www.technologyreview.com/2012/07/20/115559/a-social-network-free-of-ads/), [TechRadar](https://www.techradar.com/news/internet/web/app-net-the-ad-free-twitter-alternative-raises-over-500k-1092081)) App.net later shut down, which I know from memory, not from these pages. It shows the bet is risky, but he still took it.

**What to do:** Don't decide based on whether a leader exists. Do the work he'd ask for first:
1. List who has already tried this, including the leader and anyone who failed, and why they lost.
2. Find where the leader is stuck on something that isn't working, such as its business model, legacy customers or incentives, and that you can serve from a clean start.
3. Write down your edge: what you know or have done that others in the space haven't.

If you can answer all three clearly, he would tell you to go ahead. If your main pitch is "it's like X but better" or "cheaper," that's the tar pit he warns about.

One caveat: a YC Q&A site also quotes him saying that multiple companies in the same space is "pretty common, especially if it's a great startup idea." I couldn't trace that to the original talk, so I didn't rely on it. ([gurubase](https://gurubase.io/g/ycombinator/similar-idea-to-company-in-yc-is-this-conflict-a-problem))

Sources:

Neither. Seibel describes your situation almost word for word, and his answer is to keep the users and the problem and fix the product.

**His view**

In YC Startup School's "How to Plan an MVP" lecture (about the 3:10 mark), Seibel separates *iterating* from *pivoting*. He says founders who learn how to build something tend to fall in love with it. When it doesn't work for the users it was built for, they start asking what other problems it could solve. His analogy: you built a screwdriver that doesn't screw anything in well, so you wonder whether it could be used for cooking or cleaning. His answer:

> "Keep the mechanic, keep the problem." Then fix the screwdriver.

His point is that the mechanic and the need to screw something in aren't what's broken. The product is.

The Startup Archive version, quoted in a third-party summary of his advice, puts it the same way: *"Hold the problem you're solving tightly. Hold the customer tightly. Hold the solution you're building loosely."*

**What to do**

Stay with the users you built it for. Talk to them now and find out exactly where the MVP fails them: what they tried, where they quit, and what they do instead. Then change the product. Seibel's general MVP advice is to cut scope until you can ship in weeks, so make small changes and ship them quickly. Keep going until they actually use it. Compliments don't count as success.

Going looking for new users or new problems for the product you already have is the trap he's warning about. It feels like progress, but it means you've grown attached to the solution and dropped the problem.

**The one exception**

If those conversations show the users don't actually have this problem, or it isn't urgent for them, then the problem is what's wrong, not the product. That calls for a real pivot. Pick a new problem and start from it, not from the code you've already written. You only get to that conclusion from talking to the users, not because the first version flopped. In what I found, he doesn't give a specific trigger for when to pivot.

Sources:

Yes, for a while. Paul Graham's position is that you should go to Silicon Valley, but you don't have to stay there for good. My advice, in his spirit: move the founding team to the Bay Area for a few months (doing YC or a similar programme there is the obvious way), raise money while you're there, and then decide whether to come back to Stockholm.

**What he's said**

- **His 2007 essay "Why to Move to a Startup Hub."** His main claim is: "All other things being equal, the more of a startup hub a place is, the better startups will do there." He puts Silicon Valley at the top. He also insists "this is about cities, not countries," so it isn't a knock on Sweden. He gave the same advice to Boston startups, even though YC was based in Boston at the time. His reasons:
  - Silicon Valley investors are bolder and decide faster.
  - Deals still happen face to face.
  - Startup know-how is concentrated there.
- **His exceptions in that essay.** Staying put can make sense if you have a family, if immigration is a problem, if your industry is centred somewhere else, or if you already have a firm funding offer where you are.
- **His Stockholm talk in 2026.** YC filmed it at the Stockholm Waterfront Congress Centre in late April 2026 and released it on May 13. The title was literally "should you move to Silicon Valley," and he addressed Swedish founders directly. According to summaries of the talk, his answer was to go "for a bit and then come back." In his view that helps you and Sweden at the same time:
  - your startup gets better;
  - you bring investor money home;
  - you bring Silicon Valley's culture home.
  
  The summaries say he called coming home afterward possibly "one of the most powerful things a founder can do" for the local scene. They also list chance meetings, faster investor decisions and the "pay it forward" culture as reasons to go at least briefly.

**Why I'd pick "go temporarily"**

Staying in Stockholm the whole time means missing the advantages he says matter most early on: fast investors, dense networks and chance meetings. Moving permanently is more than he's asking for, and coming back is how Stockholm gets better as a hub. The only reason to skip the trip is one of his exceptions, such as family, a visa problem, or a solid funding offer already in hand in Stockholm.

One caveat: I couldn't find a full transcript of the Stockholm talk. The quotes from it come from secondary summaries, and some of those look AI-generated, so check the YC video before quoting him exactly. The essay quotes come from his own site.

Sources:

**Answer: No. Compete on product. That's Paul Graham's position, and it's mine too.**

**Why he would say this, from his own writing:**

1. **Brand is what's left once product differences are gone.** His essay *The Brand Age* (March 2026) uses the Swiss watch industry after the quartz crisis as its example. Its main line is "Brand is what's left when the substantive differences between products disappear." Brand-driven competition belongs to mature markets where products have converged. A startup that chooses to fight on brand is choosing to compete where it has the least to offer.

2. **He thinks branding works against good design.** He writes that "Branding isn't merely orthogonal to good design, but opposed to it," and "Branding is centrifugal; design is centripetal." Good design moves toward the right answer. Branding has to keep moving away from it to stay distinctive. He says the two can only coexist when a design space is very large or largely unexplored. Otherwise "branding can only be achieved at the expense of good design." He also tells readers to avoid "not just… buying brand, but… selling it too," and to work on real problems in fields that are "on the way up."

3. **His startup advice is about users, not image.** In *How to Get Startup Ideas* he says "by far the most common mistake startups make is to solve problems no one has." The test he proposes is "Who wants this so much that they'll use it even when it's a crappy version one?" He also says to "focus on users, not competitors." His Stripe example is that the founders "didn't have to try very hard to make themselves heard," because users were already waiting for what they built.

4. **"Make a few users love you."** *Startups in 13 Sentences* includes "Understand your users" and "Better to make a few users love you than a lot ambivalent." Brand is a way to reach many people with a thin message. Graham's model goes the other way: a small group of users who are deeply happy with something real.

**What I'd add:** Brand-age companies also tend to win on heritage, scale and money, and a startup has none of those. A startup's real advantage is speed in a field that is still changing. That's where products still differ from each other, which is exactly the situation where Graham says brand matters least. Once your product is clearly better, the reputation follows from it. Building the brand first gets that order backwards.

**The fair counterpoint:** Critics note that Apple has a valuable brand and also makes strong products, and that branding can make a category more interesting. Graham would likely say Apple earned its brand through its products, so it fits his argument. My suggestion: put your effort into the product and into understanding your users, and treat brand as the record of what you've built. Don't use it to stand in for a product that isn't better.

Sources:
- [Paul Graham, "The Brand Age"](https://paulgraham.com/brandage.html)
- [Paul Graham, "How to Get Startup Ideas"](https://paulgraham.com/startupideas.html)
- [Paul Graham, "Startups in 13 Sentences"](https://paulgraham.com/13sentences.html)
- Commentary and critiques: [byteiota](https://byteiota.com/paul-grahams-brand-age-tech-marketing-over-innovation/), [Always Be Zagging](https://abz.beehiiv.com/p/the-brand-age-isn-t-what-you-think), [zoia.org](https://zoia.org/posts/paul-graham-brand-age/), [Wisereads Vol. 134](https://wise.readwise.io/issues/wisereads-vol-134/)

His sources point to one answer: Sam Altman worries most about a quiet drift, not a robot uprising. In that future AI becomes so built into society that people lean on systems they can't understand, human and government oversight slowly weakens, and things go wrong even though nobody meant any harm.

**What he has said**

- **Federal Reserve conference, July 22, 2025.** Altman laid out three "scary categories" of AI risk:
  1. Bad actors using superintelligence, such as foreign adversaries designing a bioweapon or breaking into banks.
  2. Loss of control, the sci-fi case where AI escapes human control.
  3. Society coming to depend on AI so much that human decision-making and government oversight decline.

  He described the third as AI becoming "so ingrained in society … [that we] can't really understand what they're doing, but we do kind of have to rely on them. And even without a drop of malevolence from anyone, society can just veer off in a sort of strange direction." Lifeboat's write-up says this third one "seemed to trouble him most." That is the reporter's reading, not Altman's own ranking. Fortune adds that "emotional overreliance," especially among young people, is already showing up.
- **He puts loss of control lower.** One commentary quotes him calling the rogue-AI scenario "less of a concern to me than the first category, but a very grave concern if it came to pass."
- **He has said this for years.** At the World Governments Summit in February 2024 he said he wasn't worried about "killer robots walking on the street." He was worried that, with AI systems out in society and no ill intent, "things just go horribly wrong."

**Context**

In 2023 his warnings were vaguer or about misuse. He told the Senate his worst fear was the industry causing "significant harm to the world." He also pointed to disinformation, cyberattacks and bioweapons, and once called the worst case "lights-out for all of us." His more recent statements are sharper and keep coming back to gradual dependence. That is why I'm going with dependence over misuse or extinction.

One caveat: no source I found has Altman himself saying which of his three categories worries him most. The ranking comes from Lifeboat's description, backed up by his 2024 "no ill intent" remarks.

Sources:

## The short version: stop fundraising and go back to your customers

Seibel's core view is that raising money is not progress. In his YC post *Fundraising Rounds Are Not Milestones* he writes: **"Raising a round should be a byproduct of success. A financing round is not a milestone. It is literally cash."** He warns that treating fundraising as the goal pushes founders toward "optimizing for short term showmanship instead of making something people want." Months spent polishing a deck and going to follow-up meetings is that kind of showmanship.

In an interview he put it more bluntly: what kills startups "isn't fundraising or who you raised from. The thing that's going to kill you is that you didn't build something your customers wanted."

## What he'd tell you to do

1. **Treat the months of "maybe" as a no.** Every investor who took a meeting and didn't commit has answered a question: on what you've shown so far, the company doesn't yet look like it deserves the money. A better deck won't change that. Better traction will. His seed-pitch advice is to show traction over a time period, and if the traction is weak, leave it out rather than dress it up. So the work to do is on the business, not the slides.

2. **Cut costs until you can survive without the round.** In *Why does your company deserve more money?* he describes Justin.tv after four months of failed pitches. The team cut costs, accepted layoffs, and focused on revenue. Monthly burn went from about $250k to the company earning about $100k a month, and they finished the year with $8M in revenue and $1M in profit. His advice: "save as much money as you can, spend more time with your customers, and build a product they need." A summary of another of his talks adds that founders should try to cover their own living costs before raising.

3. **Use the break to find what's working.** Twitch came out of that period when Justin.tv stopped fundraising. Being forced to look hard at your own product and users is useful.

4. **Don't hire or spend your way to growth.** "Stop thinking that spending a lot of money and hiring a lot of employees will create growth." Staffing up only helps once you have product-market fit.

5. **Raise again when growth makes it easy.** One write-up of his talks says growth tends to bring investors to you. When you do go back out, schedule the meetings close together instead of spreading them over months. Use the two-sentence description, concrete traction over a time period, and a specific ask tied to 18–24 month milestones. Don't "limp into" a round without real growth.

## The decision

Stop the follow-up meetings this week. Spend the next stretch with users, cut burn so you aren't depending on a round to survive, and come back to investors only when you have numbers they can't ignore. Seibel's reasoning is that investors fund momentum, and months of meetings without a commitment show you don't have it yet.

A few caveats. Some of these points come from secondhand summaries of his talks rather than his own writing; the two YC/Hacker Noon essays are his own words. He also stepped back from day-to-day work at YC in March 2025.

No. Going by what Dalton Caldwell has actually said, picking a modest idea doesn't make you safer. He'd tell you to work on the ambitious idea you're obsessed with.

**What he said.** In a 2019 Y Combinator video, he says it's "almost equally hard to succeed in a startup that's a very ambitious audacious idea" as in an incremental one. He also says it's "equally hard to succeed in a startup that you don't care about and one that you do." He compares it to travel: if two places are equally far away, go to the one you're more excited about, because the excitement makes you more likely to get there. Earlier in the same video he tells founders to work on "the thing that they are very excited about and obsessed with," even if it looks harder to raise money for. His reason is that teams who don't really believe in what they're doing give up when things get rough ([Rosetta transcript](https://rosetta.to/u/ycombinator/how-do-you-convince-someone-to-join-your-startup-dalton-caldwell), [Summify](https://summify.io/discover/how-do-you-convince-someone-to-join-your-startup-dalton-cald-N8deM6/)).

**Why the "safe" idea can be the riskier one.** His main rule for founders is "just don't die" ([Lenny's Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/lessons-from-1000-yc-startups)). If you're the bottleneck for survival, an idea you don't care about raises your odds of quitting. He and Michael Seibel also warn about "tarpit ideas." These are ideas that seem doable, get early praise, and attract lots of founders, but then trap them in markets nobody can win ([Matt Rickard](https://mattrickard.com/tarpit-ideas), [Lenny's Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/lessons-from-1000-yc-startups)). An idea that feels safe and easy fits that description more often than you'd think.

**What to do:** pick the ambitious idea you can't stop thinking about, and lower the risk in how you run it rather than in what you choose. Keep the company alive, test assumptions cheaply, and pivot if you have to. Caldwell describes a good pivot as "going home," meaning toward something closer to what you're an expert in ([Lenny's Newsletter](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/lessons-from-1000-yc-startups)). One caveat: being ambitious doesn't excuse a tarpit. Before you commit, check that the big idea isn't one that lots of founders have already tried and failed at.

Sources:

Yes, Garry Tan thinks ownership matters a great deal, and his advice is to own them yourself. His line, as quoted in coverage of his Startup School 2026 talk: **"Own your skills, because if you don't, your job becomes a skill file."**

**What he said**

He tells the story of "Maya," a support engineer he made up. Over two years she teaches her agents 40 skills: handling a P0 at 2am, calming a customer who's about to leave, writing post-mortems. Those files hold two years of her judgment.
- **Version one:** the files live in her personal repo. When she changes jobs, she takes that judgment with her and starts the new role already ahead.
- **Version two:** the files live in the company's repo under IT policy. She leaves with nothing, the company keeps running on her judgment, and her name isn't even in the commit history. Tan's verdict: *"She didn't have a career. She had an extraction."*

He compares this to craftsmen, who were free because they owned their tools, and factory workers, who lost that when the loom belonged to the mill. Knowledge workers assumed their expertise was safe because it lived in their heads. Skill files take it out of your head, so someone else can now own it.

**What he does himself**

His own skill packs are public and MIT-licensed: gstack, plus GBrain, a memory system whose skills are markdown workflow files. He also argues that writing a skill file is real software design with markdown as the language, not prompt tinkering. So in his view your skill files are work product, not throwaway prompts.

**My recommendation, in his spirit**

Keep a personal skills repo that you control, starting today. Put your reusable judgment there: how you triage, debug, review, write and escalate. Keep anything that contains company data, internal systems or confidential process in the company repo.

One caveat that Tan doesn't settle: legally, most employment contracts give the employer what you create on the job. Even a sympathetic write-up says the legal question is less settled than his framing makes it sound. So read your IP agreement and don't copy company material out. Generic skills you write on your own time are the part you can realistically keep.

Also note that these quotes come from secondary write-ups and summaries of the talk, not a verbatim transcript.

**No. Stop building and launch this week with what you already have, cut down to the one problem your best users care about most.** I'm confident Michael Seibel would say this, because it's the main point of his MVP talk. The direct evidence for Dalton Caldwell is thinner; see the end.

**What Michael has said**
- His central line in YC's "How to Plan an MVP": *"launch something bad quickly."* He says the rest of the talk just restates that.
- An MVP should take *"weeks, not months"* to build. You've been building for three months, so you're already past that.
- *"First time box your spec."* If you fall behind, *"Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important."* His advice is to remove features to get something shipped, not add them.
- He calls the belief that *"feedback on the little thing is useless"* a common mistake. You learn whether the core problem is real when people react to a basic product.
- *"Please don't fall in love with your MVP."* It's *"just step one in a journey."* After launch, if the product doesn't work for a user, keep the user and their problem and fix the product.
- Summaries of his talk also say: hold the problem and the customer tightly, and hold the solution loosely.

**Why "build everything they ask for" is the wrong approach**
- Requests made on a call, about a product people aren't actually using, are opinions, not demand. Feedback from a live product is worth more.
- Each request you build makes your launch later. Claude Code makes building cheap, so the risk now is building a lot that nobody uses.
- Treat the requests as data. When several users raise the same pain point, that is probably your core problem. One-off asks go on a list for after launch.

**What Dalton has said**
- In a Dalton & Michael episode, the two of them argue that protecting your ego by not talking to users can kill your startup. Waiting until the product feels "complete" is a way of protecting your ego.
- In a 2024 YC post, Dalton says it's easy to analyze your way out of taking the first step. I only saw this in a search summary and didn't open the post.
- A secondhand summary attributes this to him: people saying they would use a product is very different from them changing their daily habits to use it. That's the case for launching: only real usage tells you which requests matter.

**What to do this week**
1. Write down the single problem that the users on your calls describe most strongly.
2. Hide or cut every feature that doesn't directly solve that problem.
3. Give it to the people from your calls now. Watch what they actually use, and build next based on usage, not on the request list.

**About the sources:** Michael's quotes come from YC's own recap of his talk, so they're solid. I couldn't find a talk where Dalton addresses launch timing or feature requests directly. His points above come from episode descriptions and secondhand summaries, and the "hold the problem tightly" line comes from a summary site, not YC's page.

Seibel would tell you to stop the letter-writing, settle on whatever your stock documents say, and move on quickly. I couldn't find anywhere he talks about lawyers trading letters, so this applies what he has said on the record to your situation.

**What he's said that applies here**

1. **The cliff is meant for exactly this, and fighting won't replace a missing one.** In his YC essay on splitting equity, he says that if you fear breaking up with a co-founder, "make sure you have a proper vesting schedule": four years with a one-year cliff. If someone leaves within the first year, they "walk away with nothing." That setup is meant to ensure "if there is a problem you can fix it without harm in year one." You're 9 months in. Under a standard cliff your co-founder would have nothing vested yet. If he really has vested shares, you either had no cliff or you credited him with earlier work. Either way, the documents decided this when you signed them. Seibel's advice is to set up protection in advance, not to claw shares back afterward.

2. **A long fight costs more than it can win you.** Looking back on his Justin.tv days, he said that when he was younger he "thought that there was value in winning the fight." He came to see that "every minute after 20 minutes where you're fighting, you're just reducing the value of your company." Also: "We know we're having a fight. It's not going to solve anything. Just stop fighting." Paying two sets of lawyers to argue over shares in a company without product-market fit is that kind of fight. The legal fees could easily cost more than the disputed stock is worth today.

3. **Control matters more than percentages.** He recommends that only the CEO hold a board seat before a big equity round. That way a decision like firing a co-founder doesn't turn into a board dispute. What you actually need from this separation is control and a clean slate, not the last few points of equity.

**What I'd do in your place**

- **Have the lawyers stop writing letters and read your stock purchase agreement.** Unvested shares go back to the company under its repurchase right. That part is mechanical, not something to negotiate.
- **Let him keep what he has actually vested.** Ask for a few things in return: a full mutual release, his IP and confidentiality obligations confirmed, his resignation from the board and any officer roles, and possibly his voting rights. If you want fewer outside shareholders, offer a small buyback. Don't litigate.
- **If "over" means the company and not just the partnership,** the dispute matters even less. Shares in a startup that's shutting down are worth roughly nothing. Wind it down cleanly and spend the money on what you do next.

Seibel would see every week you spend on this as a week you're not talking to users or building. The vested shares already cost you what they were going to cost you, and a long fight would cost you more. This is not legal advice. Have your lawyer confirm what your agreements actually say before you sign anything.

Garry Tan has published something close to a "this week" plan for exactly your situation, in a YC Root Access piece titled "Personal AGI Is How You Stay Under Your Own Power." His answer is to stop reading about agents and run one on your own computer tonight, then make it learn how you work. Here's that plan, with the decisions made for you.

**Tonight: install Claude Code and run it on your own machine.**
His first step is to "pick a harness and run an agent on your own machine." He lists OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code and Codex as options. Pick Claude Code, because his own toolkit, gstack, was built for it first. He also argues it should run on your own setup, not a rented chatbot. He defines personal AGI as an agent that "runs on your infrastructure, reads from a memory you own, executes procedures you wrote, and compounds."

**This weekend: give it context.**
Make one folder of markdown files from your notes and email, with a page for each project and person. In his view, that context is what makes an agent useful.

**Next: write one skill file for the task you hate most.**
Explain the task in plain English, let the agent get it wrong, then correct it. His test is: "If a smart intern could follow it, an agent can run it." On an a16z podcast he described a file like this as "an employee" that can do the job again and again.

**Then: schedule it, and turn every task into a skill.**
Put that skill on a recurring schedule so it runs without you. After every task, have the agent write up what it did as a reusable skill file. His rule: "If you have to ask for something twice, you failed."

**If you're a technical founder, also install gstack this week.**
gstack is his free, open-source set of Claude Code commands that act like a virtual team (CEO reviewer, designer, QA, release engineer). He suggests starting with `/office-hours`, which asks six hard questions about what you're building and writes a design doc. Then try `/plan-ceo-review` on a feature idea, `/review` on a branch of your code, and `/qa` on a staging site. After that, he says, you'll know whether it fits.

**Don't save money on usage.**
On the a16z podcast he said founders should let themselves spend heavily on agents. He estimated full-strength use at $50k–$100k a year and said that can be worth it if it speeds up how fast you try and ship things. You don't need that budget in week one, but don't throttle yourself either.

**Expect it to feel like a toy at first.**
He says week one feels like a toy, the payoff comes around week 12, and most people quit by week two. Your real job this week is to get one skill working and not quit.

**Why this is the right pick:** his whole argument is that the advantage compounds through memory and skill files you own. Researching tools doesn't build that. The only thing that does is starting the loop of doing a task, writing it down as a skill, and scheduling it.

A few caveats. The quotes come from a newsletter write-up and a news summary (Dealroom), not full transcripts. The $50k–$100k figure comes only from that one summary, and other tech leaders argue that output matters more than how many tokens you burn. Some third-party write-ups also suggest trying gstack on low-risk code first and keeping it away from production secrets.

Graham would probably push you on one thing above all: who your users are right now, and whether you can be the first payments layer they install. His newest essay is close to a brief for your company, and he seems to have posted about agent shopping three days ago. Everything below applies what he has written. He hasn't said any of it about your company.

## His main push: sign up the earliest agent startups by hand, now

In **"Making Startups Powerful"** (September 2026) he uses Stripe as his main example. Stripe signs companies up at the earliest possible moment, and they almost never leave, because *"With payments infrastructure, if it ain't broke, you don't fix it."* He also says *"selling to earlier stage companies makes you more powerful"*: if you charge by usage, your revenue grows as fast as they do. For you, that means:

- **Your customers should be agent startups at day zero**, not big merchants or enterprises. Win them before they've chosen anyone, and their growth becomes yours.
- **Use the "Collison installation."** In "Do Things That Don't Scale" he describes Stripe's founders saying *"Right then, give me your laptop"* and setting people up on the spot. Expect him to ask how many agent builders you have personally integrated this week.
- **Find the narrow, deep well.** In "How to Get Startup Ideas" he asks *"who wants this right now?"* and says to find a small group who want it a lot. "AI agents will spend trillions" is the sort of plausible-sounding pitch he calls a made-up idea. Bring a list of named users who would put up with a rough version today.

## What he'd press on next

1. **Will the model companies engulf you?** In that same essay he writes that if tokens flow through you, money does too, and the model companies become your *"component suppliers."* Then: *"The question is how easy it would be for them to engulf you, or even your customers."* Have a concrete answer for why OpenAI, Anthropic, Visa or Stripe won't just ship your product themselves.
2. **Do you own the customer relationship, or are you a component?** He asks whether a company can go *"from a mere component supplier into the one that owns the relationship with the customer."* A thin API between an agent and a merchant checkout is a component.
3. **Merchants that block agents are your opening.** On Oct 8, 2026, after Amazon introduced its agent policy, coverage quotes him saying *"People will want agents to buy stuff for them. It will be one of the main use cases"* and *"Any business that bans agents represents an opportunity for a startup to create a competitor."* He'd want to know whether your product works even when the merchant is hostile. If it only works when merchants cooperate, he'd also ask whether you should eventually go full stack and become the agent-friendly merchant yourselves.
4. **Lean into the hard, tedious parts.** In "Schlep Blindness" he calls Stripe *"the most striking example"* of founders avoiding a great idea because of bank deals, fraud and regulation. Agent payments have all of that plus questions of authorization and liability. He'd count that as an advantage, because *"everyone else will have been frightened off."* If you're skipping the compliance and fraud work, he'd tell you that work is the company.

**Bottom line:** go to office hours with the names of 10 agent startups you've installed by hand and how much money each has moved through you. That one number covers most of what he would ask.

Two caveats: I read his Amazon posts only in news coverage, not on X itself. I also didn't find anything he's said specifically about agent *payments* infrastructure, as opposed to agent shopping in general.

I couldn't find any place where Paul Graham says lean startups are dead, about AI agents running in parallel or anything else. The question seems to rest on something he didn't say. I checked his essay list, his newest essay, and his recent posts on X.

**What he has actually said**

- **On "lean startup," he says he isn't sure what it means.** In a YC interview he said he's never really been clear what a lean startup is, and admitted he hadn't read the book. That's not someone who would announce its death.
- **His newest essay doesn't touch it.** His most recent essay is "Making Startups Powerful" (September 2026). It never mentions lean startups, MVPs, or running many agents in parallel. Its question is what makes a company more powerful over time: owning the customer relationship, network effects, going full stack, building APIs, and selling to early-stage companies. Its AI points are narrower:
  - On APIs, he says to err on the side of having them, "especially now that agents are replacing human users. Who knows what they'll want to do?"
  - He wonders whether agents could pay one another.
  - He suggests letting users opt in to training your model on their interactions.
- **On X, his agent comments are about new startup openings, not methodology.** He said Amazon banning agents is the first chance since Amazon was founded for a startup to build a competitor, because people will want agents to buy things for them. He also said bot traffic is a big enough problem for several startups, one filtering agents out and another letting them in "in an orderly way."

**Where the idea probably comes from**

The "AI broke Lean" argument belongs to Steve Blank, who founded the Lean Startup movement. A July 2026 Poets & Quants piece reports Blank saying Lean needs to change and could become a fast AI-era method. That's about changing Lean, not declaring it dead, and it's Blank, not Graham. Aaron Levie's "make what agents want" idea, which borrows Graham's "make something people want," may also be getting credited to Graham. A few SEO blog posts that summarize "Graham's views on AI" add to the confusion.

**Bottom line:** If you want Graham's position, read "Making Startups Powerful." His advice is to stop asking how to iterate cheaply and ask what would make your company more powerful in a world where agents are becoming the users. In practice, that means building APIs and agent-friendly interfaces early. If someone quoted him saying "lean is dead," ask them for the link. I couldn't find one.

**His main argument: YC is a network-effects business, so its lead compounds.**

He says "it's not about the money, it's about having a community of all these people who you can trust." He also says every batch is "the top 1%" of what's going on, out of about 1% of applicants accepted. The more good founders join, the more the next good founders want in. - **Demo Day pricing.** He says YC companies are worth Demo Day prices because "you are more likely to find a multi-turn fund returner… than any other place in the world." - **AI speed.** He calls this "by far the best time in the history of startups" and cites YC companies growing "at least 10% a week for more than a year." ([Mixergy](https://mixergy.com/interviews/garry-tan-y-combinator-startups-growing-5x-faster-heres-what-changed/)) He says the difference now is that "people are actually getting commercial validation." - **Location.** He says YC startups that stay in the Bay Area become unicorns at 2.5x the rate of those that leave, because "your ambition, knowhow and access to people is a function of your environment." ([X](https://x.com/garrytan/status/1899539980940406952))

**What he'd tell you to do:** if you get into YC, take it over Speedrun, Neo, or a better-terms offer. The equity costs the same as it always has. What you get back (the network, the Demo Day investors, the company you're surrounded by) gets bigger every batch, and he says that's why YC's lead keeps growing.

Critics have challenged YC's valuations ([TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2023/04/08/were-still-talking-about-y-combinator-valuations)), and some outside guides say a16z Speedrun is now as hard to get into as YC.

No. I couldn't find any page where Dalton Caldwell recommends Portugal's Startup Visa, Lisbon, or any European visa program. Searches pairing his name with Portugal, Lisbon and Europe turned up nothing on the topic. Anyone saying he endorses it is making it up.

**What he has actually said about location:**
- In a YC video with Michael Seibel, he argues: "I don't think every startup needs to be in San Francisco to be successful." He notes that many great companies "were built outside of San Francisco" and says personal and lifestyle reasons for where you live are legitimate. Seibel takes the other side: being in a hub like the Bay Area improves your odds. ([Rosetta transcript summary](https://rosetta.to/u/ycombinator/does-your-startup-need-to-be-in-san-francisco))
- One quote in that summary cuts the other way. Asked whether he'd recommend starting outside the Bay Area, he answers "I genuinely would not," though he adds there can be good personal reasons to do so. Without the full transcript I can't tell exactly what he meant. Either way, he says nothing about visas, other countries or international founders.

**Related facts that matter for the decision:**
- YC's standard deal requires the parent company to be incorporated in the US, the Cayman Islands or Singapore. So a founder taking his kind of capital wouldn't structure the company around a Portuguese entity anyway. ([The Logic](https://thelogic.co/news/y-combinator-canada-reincorporation-startups-investors/), [Employment Hero](https://employmenthero.com/en-ca/news/y-combinator-drops-canada-investment-eligibility/), [Business Insider via The Note](https://thenote.app/post/en/y-combinator-picked-a-fight-with-canada-and-quickly-backtracked-uddx9dykmx?amp=true))
- He became YC Partner Emeritus in June 2025 and co-founded Standard Capital, a Series A firm, with Paul Buchheit and Bryan Berg. He no longer speaks for YC day to day. ([YC blog](https://www.ycombinator.com/blog/dalton-caldwell-partner-emeritus), [Forbes Peru](https://forbes.pe/negocios/2025-06-16/dos-socios-de-y-combinator-se-retiran-para-crear-un-nuevo-fondo-de-serie-a/), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton_Caldwell))

**What I'd conclude from his record:** don't treat a visa program as your company strategy. His position is that a city doesn't make or break a startup, but he's never singled out Lisbon. If you want to live in Portugal, you can use the Startup Visa for your own residency. It's run by IAPMEI, needs approval from a certified incubator, and gives a two-year permit you can renew ([Wise](https://wise.com/gb/blog/portugal-startup-visa), [Startup Portugal](https://startupportugal.com/?p=81)). If you plan to raise US venture money, incorporate the parent company in Delaware, and don't attribute the Lisbon choice to him.

I couldn't find anything Garry Tan has said or done about raising the Reg CF cap, or about whether founders should use Reg CF instead of SAFEs. I won't put a position in his mouth that I can't source. The pick below is my own view.

**What I searched.** I ran several searches combining his name with Regulation Crowdfunding, the SEC, accredited-investor rules, and the platforms Wefunder, Republic and StartEngine. None returned a statement from him. The only filing of his with the SEC that turned up is a 2018 letter supporting the Long-Term Stock Exchange (LTSE), which has nothing to do with crowdfunding. The one article I could open about the current petition doesn't mention him or Y Combinator. I couldn't open the SEC's comment list for the petition, so I can't rule out a comment from him there.

**Where the cap stands.**
- The SEC caps Reg CF raises at $5 million per 12 months.
- Crowdfund Capital Advisors, whose founder Sherwood Neiss helped write the original crowdfunding framework, petitioned the SEC to raise it to $20 million with inflation indexing. It is File No. 4-914, first sent in January 2026 and refiled in July 2026.
- The petition refers to a separate petition seeking the same increase (File No. 4-889). One article says the CEOs of Wefunder, Republic and StartEngine co-signed it. Sources disagree on which file is which, so treat that detail as unconfirmed.
- Most public comments so far support the increase. I found no SEC decision.

**My pick: use a SAFE for a normal seed round. Treat Reg CF as an extra, not a replacement.**
- **The cap isn't what's holding seed founders back.** Most seed rounds are well under $5 million, so going to $20 million mainly helps companies past the seed stage.
- **Reg CF costs more.** One article reports the platforms take 6–8% of what you raise, and another says Republic charges 7% in cash plus 2% in securities. Reg CF also requires an SEC filing and annual reports afterward. A post-money SAFE is a free standard document. It also lets you see your dilution when you sign: raising $1 million on a $10 million cap means you've sold 10%.
- **Follow-on investors know SAFEs.** About 85% of SAFEs signed in 2024 were post-money, so seed and Series A investors already know the terms.
- **When Reg CF does make sense:** if you have a consumer product with loyal customers who want to own a piece, a community round on top of your SAFE round can work well. Even then, the security is often a SAFE-style instrument sold through the portal, so it's not really an either/or choice.

To learn what Tan himself thinks, ask him directly on X or look for any comments filed under SEC File No. 4-914 or 4-889.

I couldn't find her saying that, and her own statements say the opposite. In her published account of founding YC, Livingston says early YC filtered out the kind of founder the question describes. Where she does use the words "aggressive" and "ruthless," she's talking about investors, and as a contrast to herself.

**What she said she screened for**

From "9 Things She Learned From Founding YC" (2018):
- "From the beginning, I was very careful about only funding earnest people."
- "I always tried to create an asshole-free culture." And: "If I could tell someone was a conceited asshole, we did not fund them." She says this strictness is "the basis of the culture of our alumni community."
- The questions she asked about applicants were "Did they seem earnest?", "Did they seem determined?" and "Were they flexible-minded?"

**Where "aggressive" and "ruthless" come from**

She describes herself as "soft and sensitive at a time when investors tended to be hardened and aggressive," and adds, "I'll throw in ruthless too for a couple of them that I know." Those are investors she was defining herself against. She calls her own role being YC's "mom": counseling overwhelmed founders and settling co-founder disputes.

**Paul Graham's account agrees**

In his essay about her, Graham says she has "x-ray vision for character" and "can see through any kind of faker almost immediately." He also says YC would "refuse to fund founders whose characters we had doubts about even if we thought they'd be successful." So YC was willing to pass on likely winners with bad character, which is the opposite of backing ruthless people because they win.

**What she does think wins**

Determination. She calls it the single most important quality in a founder and ranks it above intelligence. Her reasoning is that talented founders often fail because they can't keep going when things get hard. She also says founders need to commit fully, to "burn the boat." That's about persistence, not about how founders treat other people.

**Bottom line:** The quote is probably a mix-up of "determined" with "ruthless," or of her description of investors with her description of founders. If you want to describe her view accurately, say early YC backed earnest, determined, flexible founders and deliberately turned down jerks, even promising ones. That's what she and Graham both say on the record.
